intervals.label: construction
intervals.note: Davis's Nobel lecture also shows the experiment's chamber half-excavated in the summer of 1965.
intervals.quote: The Homestake solar neutrino experiment was built in the period 1965–1967

intervals.label: operation
intervals.locator: Davis, Nobel Lecture 2002, p. 68, paragraph after Fig. 7; end: Davis, Nobel autobiography (Les Prix Nobel 2002), paragraph beginning 'I retired from Brookhaven in 1984'; SURF, Our Story
intervals.note: Start: the year Davis gives for the experiment becoming operational; the standard data set analysed by Cleveland et al. begins in 1970, when rise-time counting was introduced. End of operation: Davis writes that the experiment "continued to measure the solar neutrino flux until the late 1990s, when the Homestake Mine ceased operating"; SURF dates the end of the mine's operation to 2001, and Cleveland et al. (accepted October 1997) still describe the detector as measuring solar neutrinos. The date is therefore bounded between 1997 and 2001 and marked approximate; no source read gives the date of the last extraction. The standard data set of 108 observations ends in 1994, which is not the end of operation.
intervals.quote: The Homestake experiment became operational in 1967.

intervals.label: shut down
intervals.locator: Davis, Nobel autobiography (Les Prix Nobel 2002), paragraph beginning 'I retired from Brookhaven in 1984'; SURF, Our Story, 'The Unique History of the Black Hills'
intervals.note: Davis: "The experiment continued to measure the solar neutrino flux until the late 1990s, when the Homestake Mine ceased operating." SURF says the mine operated until 2001, so the date is bounded between 1997 (Cleveland et al. still describe ongoing measurements) and 2001 and marked approximate. The standard data set of 108 observations ends in 1994, which is not the end of operation.
intervals.quote: The experiment continued to measure the solar neutrino flux until the late 1990s, when the Homestake Mine ceased operating.

name: Homestake chlorine detector
notes: Coordinate caveat: the site referenced (site:surf-surface-campus) is a surface campus point, not the detector's true ~1478 m underground location; see placement note.

placements.note: site:surf-surface-campus is an approximate campus-level point for the whole SURF/Homestake site, used because no distinct sourced coordinate exists for the Davis chlorine-tank chamber. The detector was actually ~1478 m (4850 ft) underground, not at the surface; the placement's role is sourced from the 1998 paper, its dates from the experiment's intervals (the end is approximate, late 1990s), but the site point only marks the general campus location, not the true underground depth.
placements.quote: The Homestake Solar Neutrino Observatory is located in the Homestake Gold Mine, at Lead, South Dakota

target_mass.locator: Nobel Committee for Physics, Advanced information on the Nobel Prize in Physics 2002, section "Neutrino astronomy" (paragraph on the Davis experiment in the Homestake Gold Mine)
target_mass.note: Mass of the perchloroethylene (C2Cl4) filling as stated by the Nobel Committee for Physics; the volume of the same tank (100,000 gallons) is given in Davis's Nobel lecture.
target_mass.quote: The tank contained 615 tonnes of C2Cl4, an agent normally used for dry cleaning.

summary.plain: A tank of dry-cleaning fluid, nearly a mile underground, that turned rare chlorine atoms into argon whenever a solar neutrino struck.
summary.technical: Radiochemical chlorine-argon detector, 380 m³ perchloroethylene target, 1478 m (4850 ft) underground in the Homestake mine; built 1965-1967, operational from 1967 (standard data set 1970-1994), measured 37Ar production rate 2.56±0.16(stat)±0.16(syst) SNU.

technology.note: Reaction νe + 37Cl → 37Ar + e⁻ (inverse beta decay) and the extraction/counting steps: Cleveland et al. 1998 abstract (src:homestake-1998-flux-measurement). Perchloroethylene tank, argon extraction by helium sweep every two to three months: Davis Nobel lecture (quoted). The 'dry-cleaning fluid' gloss: Davis's Nobel autobiography calls perchloroethylene 'a solvent most commonly used for dry cleaning of clothing' (src:vf-davis-nobel-biographical-2002).
technology.quote: build a 100,000-gallon chlorine-argon neutrino detector in the Homestake Gold Mine ... In order to extract argon from the tank, helium is bubbled through the perchloroethylene.
technology.value: Radiochemical chlorine detector: solar neutrinos capture on 37Cl to produce 37Ar via inverse beta decay in a large tank of perchloroethylene (dry-cleaning fluid), with the argon periodically extracted and counted
